etymology: From the superscription “A Psalm of David”; the twenty-third in the Psalter, known from its first words as “The LORD is my shepherd.”
biblical_def: Psalm 23 is the best loved of all the psalms, a song of David in which the shepherd-king confesses the LORD to be his own Shepherd. In six brief verses it unfolds the whole care of God over His people. The Shepherd supplies every need, so that the believer shall not want; He leads to green pastures and still waters and restores the soul; He guides in the paths of righteousness for His name’s sake. Even in the valley of the shadow of death the sheep fears no evil, for the Shepherd is present, and His rod and staff comfort. The figure then changes to a host who spreads a table in the presence of enemies, anoints the head with oil, and fills the cup to overflowing. The psalm closes in settled assurance: goodness and mercy shall follow all the days of life, and the believer shall dwell in the house of the LORD for ever. The Lord Jesus takes up this very image when He calls Himself the Good Shepherd who gives His life for the sheep. The dictionary receives the psalm not as a sentimental comfort merely, but as a confession of the sovereign, particular, persevering care of God for every one of His own, from the green pasture of this life to the everlasting house of the next.
webster_summary: David’s beloved psalm confessing the LORD as Shepherd, who supplies, restores, guides, and comforts His people through death itself to the house of the LORD for ever.
webster_full: PSALM 23, the psalm of David beginning “The LORD is my shepherd.”
Confesses the LORD as Shepherd who supplies every need, so the believer shall not want.
Leads to green pastures and still waters and restores the soul.
Gives no fear in the valley of the shadow of death, for the Shepherd is present.
Closes in the assurance of dwelling in the house of the LORD for ever.
scriptures: Psa 23:1
The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
Psa 23:4
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
Psa 23:6
Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
corruption_summary: The psalm is sentimentalized into a vague comfort, severed from the sovereign Shepherd and the particular care it confesses.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the comfort of Psalm 23 rests wholly on the character and sovereignty of the Shepherd. “I shall not want” is not a promise of ease but of sufficiency: the sheep lacks nothing because the Shepherd supplies all. Modern sentiment reduces the psalm to a soothing poem read at funerals; the believer must recover it as a bold confession of the particular, persevering care of God over each of His own.

Where a corruption presses, it is the detaching of the psalm from Christ. The Lord Jesus claims the very image: “I am the good shepherd.” The valley of the shadow of death holds no terror because the Shepherd Himself passed through death for the sheep and rose again. To read the psalm without Him is to keep the comfort while losing its ground; the rod and staff that comfort are held by nail-pierced hands.
roots_summary: The psalm draws on the shepherd imagery deep in Israel’s life, fulfilled in Christ the Good Shepherd.
roots_lines: Hebrew rō’eh — a shepherd, one who tends and feeds the flock.
Hebrew nāḥam and kindred terms — to comfort, console, the comfort of rod and staff.
The “valley of the shadow of death,” Hebrew tsalmaveth, deep darkness.
The shepherd figure runs from Abel and the patriarchs to David to Christ.
Greek poimēn — shepherd, the title Jesus claims in John 10.
usage: Psalm 23 is read at deathbeds and funerals for its assurance through the valley of death.
It is preached as the confession of God’s particular, persevering care for each believer.
Its shepherd imagery is connected with Christ’s claim to be the Good Shepherd.

etymology: From the superscription, a psalm of David “when Nathan the prophet came unto him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba”; the great penitential psalm.
biblical_def: Psalm 51 is the great penitential psalm, David’s cry of repentance after the prophet Nathan confronted him over his sin with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah. It is the model of evangelical repentance for the whole church. David appeals first to the mercy and lovingkindness of God, not to any merit of his own, pleading to be washed and cleansed from his iniquity. He owns his sin without excuse—“against thee, thee only, have I sinned”—and traces it to its root in a fallen nature, confessing that he was shapen in iniquity and conceived in sin, the classic Scripture for original sin. He prays not merely for pardon but for renewal: “Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me,” knowing that no outward sacrifice avails, but only a broken and a contrite heart, which God will not despise. The psalm joins justification and sanctification, pardon and cleansing, in one believing prayer. The dictionary holds Psalm 51 as the anatomy of true repentance: it goes deeper than the act to the nature, despairs of self-righteousness, casts itself wholly on mercy, and asks God to do the renewing work that the sinner cannot do for himself. It is the prayer of every believer brought low by his sin.
webster_summary: David’s great penitential psalm after his sin with Bathsheba; the church’s model of evangelical repentance, owning sin, confessing original corruption, and pleading for a clean heart.
webster_full: PSALM 51, the penitential psalm of David after Nathan confronted his sin.
Appeals to God’s mercy and lovingkindness, not to any merit of David’s own.
Owns sin without excuse: “against thee, thee only, have I sinned.”
Traces sin to its root: “in sin did my mother conceive me,” the text for original sin.
Prays for renewal: “Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
scriptures: Psa 51:1
Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.
Psa 51:4
Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.
Psa 51:5
Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.
Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
corruption_summary: Repentance is reduced to regret over consequences, and the psalm’s confession of original sin is denied.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the depth of true repentance. David does not merely regret his ruin or fear exposure; he owns the evil as against God Himself, traces it to the corruption of his nature, and pleads for cleansing he cannot accomplish. Against a therapy-culture that reframes sin as a mistake, a wound, or a stage of growth, Psalm 51 names sin as sin and casts the soul wholly on the mercy of God.

A direct corruption denies the psalm’s teaching on original sin: “in sin did my mother conceive me.” The modern doctrine of native innocence cannot abide this confession and explains it away as poetic exaggeration. The dictionary holds with David and with Paul that sin is not merely the sum of our acts but the corruption of our nature from conception, and that the only remedy is the creating word of God—“Create in me a clean heart”—the same word that made the worlds and raises the dead.
roots_summary: The psalm’s vocabulary of washing, blotting, and creating sets forth the cleansing and renewing work of God in repentance.
roots_lines: Hebrew ḥānan — to be gracious, the plea “have mercy” that opens the psalm.
Hebrew kābas — to wash thoroughly, as a fuller washes cloth; “wash me.”
Hebrew bārā’ — to create, the verb used of God alone; “create in me a clean heart.”
Hebrew dākāh — to be crushed, contrite; the broken and contrite heart God will not despise.
The superscription ties the psalm to the historical sin recorded in 2 Samuel.
usage: Psalm 51 is the church’s standard model of evangelical repentance and confession.
Verse five is the principal Old Testament text for the doctrine of original sin.
The prayer for a clean heart is used to teach that renewal is God’s creative work, not self-reform.

etymology: The ninety-first psalm, known from its opening as “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High”; a psalm of confidence in God’s protection.
biblical_def: Psalm 91 is the great psalm of divine protection, a song of confidence in the LORD as the refuge and fortress of His people. It opens with the secret place of the most High and the shadow of the Almighty, and promises deliverance from the snare of the fowler, the noisome pestilence, the terror by night, and the arrow that flieth by day. He that trusts in God shall not be afraid, though a thousand fall at his side, for the LORD is his habitation, and He shall give His angels charge to keep him in all his ways. The psalm must be read with care, for the devil himself quoted its promise of angelic guardianship when he tempted Christ to cast Himself from the temple, and the Lord answered, “Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.” The promise is not a charm against all bodily harm, nor a license to presume upon God, but the covenant assurance that no evil shall finally befall the one who dwells in God—that the believer is kept for an end, body and soul, in life and in death. The dictionary receives Psalm 91 as the believer’s confidence in the particular providence of God, rightly understood: not exemption from all suffering, but the certainty that the saint is hidden in the Almighty and shall be brought safely home.
webster_summary: The psalm of divine protection, confessing the LORD as refuge and fortress; rightly read not as a charm against all harm but as covenant assurance that no evil shall finally befall the believer.
webster_full: PSALM 91, the psalm of confidence in God’s protection.
Opens with the secret place of the most High and the shadow of the Almighty.
Promises deliverance from the snare, the pestilence, the terror by night, the arrow by day.
Its angel promise was quoted by Satan in tempting Christ, and answered by Him.
Assures not exemption from suffering but that no evil shall finally befall the believer.
scriptures: Psa 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
Psa 91:2
I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust.
For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.
Mat 4:7
Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.
corruption_summary: The psalm is twisted into a guarantee of bodily safety or a magic charm, the very presumption the devil urged on Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the right reading of the promise. Satan himself quoted Psalm 91 to tempt the Lord to a presumptuous leap, and Christ refused: to claim God’s protection while running into needless danger is not faith but tempting God. The psalm assures the believer who dwells in God, walks in his appointed ways, and trusts the Almighty—not the presumptuous who demand exemption from all harm on their own terms.

Where a corruption presses, it is the health-and-prosperity misuse that reads the psalm as a blanket guarantee against sickness, accident, and death. Saints have suffered and died trusting these very words; martyrs have gone to the stake with Psalm 91 on their lips. The promise is deeper than the body’s safety: no evil shall finally befall the one who is hidden in God, for even death is swallowed up in the keeping of the Almighty, and the believer is brought through every danger safely home.
roots_summary: The psalm’s images of refuge, fortress, and shadow gather the covenant assurance of dwelling safely in God.
roots_lines: Hebrew maḥseh — a refuge, shelter, place of safety; “he is my refuge.”
Hebrew metsudah — a fortress, stronghold; the LORD as the believer’s defense.
Hebrew tsel — shadow, shade; “the shadow of the Almighty,” nearness and covering.
Hebrew Shadday — the Almighty, the all-sufficient God.
The angelic charge of verse 11 is cited and rightly bounded by Christ in the wilderness.
usage: Psalm 91 is a favorite of soldiers and the persecuted for its confidence in God’s keeping.
Christ’s answer to Satan’s misuse of it guards against presuming upon God.
It is preached as covenant assurance, not a guarantee of bodily exemption from suffering.

etymology: A psalm of David; the most quoted Old Testament chapter in the New Testament, setting forth the Messiah as both King and Priest.
biblical_def: Psalm 110 is the most frequently cited Old Testament chapter in the New Testament, a psalm of David in which he foresees the Messiah as both King and Priest. It opens, “The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool”—words the Lord Jesus used to silence the Pharisees, asking how David could call his own son Lord, unless the Messiah were more than David’s son. The psalm sets the Messiah at the right hand of God in royal session, ruling in the midst of His enemies, leading a willing people in the day of His power. Then it joins to His kingship an everlasting priesthood: “The LORD hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek”—a priesthood older than Aaron’s and abiding for ever, the very text the Epistle to the Hebrews expounds at length. Here King and Priest, throne and altar, meet in one person. The dictionary receives Psalm 110 as a pillar of New Testament Christology: it proves the deity of the Messiah, His present session and reign at God’s right hand, His unending priestly intercession, and the certainty of His final triumph over every enemy. David’s Lord is enthroned, and His priesthood never fails.
webster_summary: David’s psalm, the most quoted Old Testament chapter in the New, setting the Messiah at God’s right hand as King and as everlasting Priest after the order of Melchizedek.
webster_full: PSALM 110, the psalm of David most cited in the New Testament.
Opens, “The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand.”
Used by Christ to prove the Messiah is more than David’s son.
Sets the Messiah in royal session, ruling in the midst of His enemies.
Joins kingship to an everlasting priesthood after the order of Melchizedek.
scriptures: The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
The LORD hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.
The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool?
Heb 7:17
For he testifieth, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec.
corruption_summary: The psalm’s witness to the Messiah’s deity and priesthood is dissolved by critics who deny David’s authorship and its predictive force.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the psalm’s plain Christology, established by the Lord Jesus Himself. He pressed the Pharisees with its opening verse: if David in the Spirit calls Messiah “my Lord,” the Christ is no mere descendant of David but David’s divine Lord enthroned at God’s right hand. The psalm proves at once the deity, the royal session, and the unending priesthood of Christ.

Where modern handling errs, it is in the critical denial of Davidic authorship and the refusal of genuine prediction, reading the psalm as a court poem for an earthly king with no Messianic reach. But the New Testament writers, following Christ, quote it constantly as fulfilled in Him: His present reign, His intercession as our great High Priest, and the certainty that every enemy shall be made His footstool. To empty the psalm of its prophecy is to silence the chapter Heaven quotes most.
roots_summary: The psalm binds the Messiah’s royal session at God’s right hand to His everlasting Melchizedek priesthood.
roots_lines: Hebrew n’um YHWH — “the oracle of the LORD,” the solemn divine utterance opening the psalm.
Hebrew ’ādōn — lord, master; David calls the Messiah “my Lord.”
Melchizedek — the priest-king of Salem, whose order the Messiah’s priesthood follows.
The “right hand” — the place of honor, power, and royal session.
Hebrews 5 through 7 expounds the Melchizedek priesthood of verse 4.
usage: Psalm 110 is a foundational proof-text for the deity and present reign of Christ.
Its priestly verse is expounded at length in the Epistle to the Hebrews.
Christ’s use of verse one is cited to confound the denial of His divine sonship.

etymology: “A Song of degrees for Solomon”; the psalm that begins “Except the LORD build the house.”
biblical_def: Psalm 127 is one of the Songs of degrees, ascribed to Solomon, teaching that all human labor is vain apart from the blessing of God. “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.” The builder, the watchman, the early riser who eats the bread of sorrows—all toil to no purpose unless God gives the increase; for He gives His beloved sleep, the rest of trust rather than the anxiety of self-reliance. The second half of the psalm turns to the family and declares children to be the gift and heritage of the LORD: “Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward. As arrows are in the hand of a mighty man; so are children of the youth. Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them.” The two halves are one: the house God builds is not only the dwelling but the household, the family and its generations, and these too are His gift, not man’s achievement. The dictionary receives Psalm 127 as the charter of God-dependent labor and of the biblical welcome of children. Against an age that prizes self-made success and treats children as a burden to be limited, the psalm names them a heritage, a reward, and a quiver of arrows—a blessing the LORD bestows on those who fear Him.
webster_summary: Solomon’s psalm teaching that all labor is vain without the LORD’s blessing, and declaring children to be a heritage and reward from God, a full quiver of arrows.
webster_full: PSALM 127, a Song of degrees ascribed to Solomon.
“Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it.”
Teaches that toil and watching are vain without God’s blessing.
“He giveth his beloved sleep”—the rest of trust over anxious self-reliance.
Declares children the heritage and reward of the LORD, a full quiver of arrows.
scriptures: Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.
Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.
Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them: they shall not be ashamed, but they shall speak with the enemies in the gate.
corruption_summary: The psalm’s welcome of children as a heritage is inverted by a culture that treats them as a burden to be limited or avoided.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold: that labor without God’s blessing is vain, and that children are a heritage of the LORD. Against the gospel of self-made success that rises early and sits up late trusting its own striving, the psalm sets the rest of faith—“he giveth his beloved sleep.” The believer works diligently but rests in God, knowing the increase is His to give.

A direct corruption presses against the second half of the psalm. An age that prizes autonomy and comfort recasts children as a cost, a limitation, an obstacle to self-fulfillment, and esteems the empty quiver wiser than the full. Scripture says the opposite: children are a heritage, a reward, and arrows in the hand of a mighty man. The dictionary holds the psalm’s plain blessing, naming the modern flight from fruitfulness as a refusal of one of God’s appointed gifts.
roots_summary: The psalm joins the building of the house to the gift of children, both named the LORD’s own work and reward.
roots_lines: Hebrew bayith — house, both the building and the household or family that fills it.
Hebrew naḥalah — an inheritance, heritage; children are the LORD’s heritage.
Hebrew sākār — reward, wages; the fruit of the womb is His reward.
The “Song of degrees” — a pilgrim psalm sung on the ascent to Jerusalem.
The arrows and quiver picture children as strength and defense for the godly home.
usage: Psalm 127 is preached to teach God-dependent labor against anxious self-reliance.
Its declaration that children are a heritage grounds the biblical welcome of children.
The full-quiver image is cited in discussions of family and fruitfulness.

etymology: The ninth chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans; the great Scripture on the sovereignty of God in election.
biblical_def: Romans 9 is the fullest treatment in Scripture of the sovereignty of God in election and reprobation. Paul, grieving over unbelieving Israel, defends the faithfulness of God by showing that the promise was never to all Israel after the flesh but to the children of promise. He proves God’s free choice from the patriarchs: before Jacob and Esau were born, having done neither good nor evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, it was said, “Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.” The choice rests not on works nor on foreseen faith but on Him that calleth. To the objection that this is unjust, Paul answers that God said to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy,” so that it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. He raised up Pharaoh to display His power, and He hardens whom He will. To the further objection, “Why doth he yet find fault?” Paul does not soften but presses: shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus? The potter has power over the clay. The dictionary receives Romans 9 as the clearest charter of unconditional election: salvation is of the Lord, His mercy is free and sovereign, and the creature has no claim upon the Creator but owes Him everything.
webster_summary: Paul’s fullest treatment of God’s sovereignty in election; salvation rests not on works or foreseen faith but on God who shows mercy, the Potter over the clay.
webster_full: ROMANS 9, the great chapter on the sovereignty of God in election.
Shows the promise was to the children of promise, not all Israel after the flesh.
Proves free election from Jacob and Esau, chosen before they had done good or evil.
“I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy”—mercy is free and sovereign.
The Potter has power over the clay; the creature owes the Creator everything.
scriptures: Rom 9:11
(For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth;)
Rom 9:15
For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion.
Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
Rom 9:21
Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?
corruption_summary: The chapter’s sovereign election is evaded by reading it as merely national, or as resting on foreseen faith, against Paul’s own argument.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is unconditional election. Paul forecloses every escape: the choice of Jacob over Esau was made before they were born or had done any good or evil, expressly that election might rest on Him that calleth and not on works. To make election depend on foreseen faith or merit is to assert the very thing the chapter denies.

A common evasion reads Romans 9 as concerned only with national destiny—the choice of Israel as a people for an earthly role—and not with the eternal salvation of individuals. But Paul’s grief is over individuals perishing in unbelief, his examples are individuals, and his conclusion is the mercy and hardening of individuals by the sovereign will of God. The dictionary holds the chapter’s plain force, including its hard sayings: God has mercy on whom He will and hardens whom He will, and the clay may not answer back to the Potter.
roots_summary: The chapter’s language of calling, mercy, and the potter sets forth God’s free and sovereign election.
roots_lines: Greek eklogē — election, choice; “the purpose of God according to election.”
Greek eleō — to have mercy; “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.”
Greek sklērunō — to harden; “whom he will he hardeneth.”
The potter and clay image draws on Isaiah and Jeremiah.
“Children of promise” distinguishes the elect from Israel after the flesh.
usage: Romans 9 is the central New Testament text for unconditional election.
Its potter-and-clay image is cited for the Creator’s sovereign right over the creature.
It is preached against schemes that ground election in foreseen faith or works.

etymology: The closing chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans; a chapter of greetings to named saints and households.
biblical_def: Romans 16 is the closing chapter of Paul’s great epistle, a long roll of greetings to named believers in the church at Rome, with a final warning and a soaring doxology. Far from a mere postscript, it is a precious window into the life of the early church. Paul commends Phebe, a servant of the church at Cenchrea, who bore the epistle; he greets Priscilla and Aquila, who had laid down their own necks for his life; he salutes whole households, kinsmen, fellow-prisoners, beloved laborers, and the church that met in a house. The chapter shows the warmth, particularity, and breadth of Christian fellowship—men and women, slave and free, Jew and Gentile, all one in Christ and named with affection. Paul adds a sharp warning to mark and avoid those who cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine learned, for such serve their own belly and by good words deceive the simple. The epistle closes with a doxology to the only wise God, who is able to establish the saints according to the gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ. The dictionary receives Romans 16 as a portrait of the household of faith: doctrine issues in love, the gospel gathers a named and varied people, and the same apostle who expounded sovereign grace knew and loved his brethren by name.
webster_summary: The closing chapter of Romans, a roll of affectionate greetings to named saints and households, with a warning against divisive teachers and a doxology to the only wise God.
webster_full: ROMANS 16, the closing chapter of Paul’s epistle to the Romans.
A long roll of greetings to named believers and households in the church at Rome.
Commends Phebe, a servant of the church, and greets Priscilla and Aquila.
Warns the saints to mark and avoid those who cause divisions contrary to sound doctrine.
Closes with a doxology to the only wise God who establishes the saints.
scriptures: Rom 16:1
I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea:
Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you.
Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them.
To God only wise, be glory through Jesus Christ for ever. Amen.
corruption_summary: The chapter’s named greetings are mined to overturn the order of the church, reading honored fellow-laborers as proof of women in the ruling office.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption presses the named women of Romans 16—Phebe, Priscilla, Junia, and the rest—into an argument that Scripture sanctions women in the offices of teaching and ruling elder. The chapter honors these women warmly as servants, helpers, fellow-laborers, and hosts of the church, and the dictionary honors them too; the gospel dignifies and employs women in countless vital labors. But commendation as a fellow-worker is not appointment to the eldership, which Paul elsewhere reserves to qualified men, and the same apostle who greets these women wrote that he suffered not a woman to teach nor to usurp authority over the man.

The honest reading neither erases these women nor unmakes the order of the church. Phebe carried the epistle; Priscilla helped instruct Apollos; many women labored much in the Lord. The dictionary celebrates this without conscripting it for egalitarian revolt. The chapter’s real lesson is the breadth and warmth of the household of faith—a named and varied people, men and women together, gathered by sovereign grace and bound in love—and its closing warning to avoid those who divide the church contrary to the doctrine once learned.
roots_summary: The chapter’s greetings and commendations display the named fellowship of the early church and its bonds of love.
roots_lines: Greek aspazomai — to greet, salute; the verb that runs through the chapter’s roll of names.
Greek diakonos — servant, minister; Phebe a servant of the church at Cenchrea.
Greek sunergos — fellow-worker; Paul’s frequent title for his helpers.
The “holy kiss” — a customary greeting of affection among the early saints.
The closing doxology names the “only wise God” who establishes believers.
usage: Romans 16 is cited to show the warmth and breadth of early Christian fellowship.
Its warning against divisive teachers is applied to guarding the church’s unity in truth.
The named women are honored as laborers while the eldership remains reserved to men.

etymology: The seventh chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews; the exposition of Christ’s priesthood after the order of Melchizedek.
biblical_def: Hebrews 7 is the great chapter on the priesthood of Christ after the order of Melchizedek, expounding the brief account of Melchizedek in Genesis and the oath of Psalm 110. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the most high God, met Abraham and blessed him and received tithes from him; being without recorded father, mother, or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, he is made like unto the Son of God, a priest continually. The chapter argues the superiority of this priesthood to that of Aaron: Levi, still in the loins of Abraham, paid tithes to Melchizedek and was blessed by him, and the lesser is blessed by the greater. The Levitical priesthood could make nothing perfect, and was changed; Christ’s priesthood is established by the divine oath, “Thou art a priest for ever,” and abides unchangeable because He continueth ever. Therefore He is able to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by Him, seeing He ever liveth to make intercession for them. Such a high priest became us, holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, who needs not to offer sacrifice daily, for this He did once when He offered up Himself. The dictionary receives Hebrews 7 as the charter of Christ’s eternal, perfect, interceding priesthood, which fulfills and abolishes the Aaronic shadow and secures the everlasting salvation of His people.
webster_summary: The chapter expounding Christ’s eternal priesthood after the order of Melchizedek, superior to Aaron’s, established by oath, abiding unchangeable, saving to the uttermost.
webster_full: HEBREWS 7, the exposition of Christ’s Melchizedek priesthood.
Draws on Melchizedek in Genesis and the oath of Psalm 110.
Shows this priesthood superior to Aaron’s: Levi paid tithes in Abraham.
Established by the divine oath, “Thou art a priest for ever.”
Christ saves to the uttermost, ever living to make intercession.
scriptures: Heb 7:24
But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood.
Heb 7:25
Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.
Heb 7:26
For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens;
Heb 7:27
Who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people’s: for this he did once, when he offered up himself.
corruption_summary: Christ’s once-for-all priesthood is obscured by any scheme of repeated sacrifice or continuing human priesthood.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is the doctrine of a continuing sacrificing priesthood and a repeated offering, against which Hebrews 7 stands as a direct rebuke. The Roman Mass, in which Christ is said to be offered again and again upon the altar, and the human priesthood that claims to offer it, contradict the chapter’s plain teaching: Christ offered up Himself once, He has an unchangeable priesthood that passes to no successor, and by one offering He has perfected for ever them that are sanctified.

The dictionary names the corruption precisely and holds the chapter’s argument. The Levitical priests were many, because death prevented them from continuing; Christ continues ever, and His priesthood is untransferable. There is no need of daily sacrifice, for the one self-offering is complete; there is no need of an earthly mediating priesthood, for the believer comes to God directly through the one High Priest who ever lives to intercede. The finished work and the abiding intercession of Christ are the soul’s whole security.
roots_summary: The chapter binds Melchizedek, the divine oath, and Christ’s endless life into one perfect and abiding priesthood.
roots_lines: Melchizedek — “king of righteousness,” then king of Salem, “king of peace,” priest of the most high God.
Greek aparabatos — unchangeable, untransferable; Christ’s priesthood passes to no successor.
Greek eis to pantelēs — “to the uttermost,” completely and for ever.
Greek entunchanō — to intercede; Christ ever lives to make intercession.
The oath of Psalm 110:4 grounds the permanence of the priesthood.
usage: Hebrews 7 is the central text for the eternal, once-for-all priesthood of Christ.
Its “save to the uttermost” assures the perseverance of those Christ intercedes for.
It is cited against repeated sacrifice and a continuing human sacrificing priesthood.

etymology: The fifty-eighth chapter of Isaiah; the LORD’s rebuke of hollow fasting and His call to true fasting and Sabbath-keeping.
biblical_def: Isaiah 58 is the LORD’s searching word on the difference between hollow religion and true godliness, spoken to a people who fasted and afflicted their souls yet wondered why God took no notice. The LORD exposes the emptiness of their fast: they fasted for strife and debate, to smite with the fist of wickedness, while oppressing their laborers and pleasing themselves. He then describes the fast that He has chosen—to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo heavy burdens, to let the oppressed go free, to deal bread to the hungry, to bring the poor to one’s house, to cover the naked, and not to hide oneself from one’s own flesh. To such obedience He attaches great promise: light breaking forth as the morning, healing, the answered cry, guidance, and renewed strength. The chapter then turns to the Sabbath, calling the people to turn away their foot from doing their pleasure on the holy day, to call it a delight, and to honor the LORD, with the promise that they should then delight themselves in the LORD and ride upon the high places of the earth. The dictionary receives Isaiah 58 as the great Scripture on sincere religion: God despises the form of fasting and Sabbath-keeping divorced from mercy and obedience, and delights in the worship that flows from a changed heart into works of justice and love.
webster_summary: The LORD’s rebuke of hollow fasting and His description of the fast He chooses—mercy, justice, and care for the needy—joined to a call to delight in the Sabbath.
webster_full: ISAIAH 58, the LORD’s word on true and false fasting.
Exposes the empty fast of a people who afflict the soul yet oppress their laborers.
Describes the chosen fast: to free the oppressed, feed the hungry, clothe the naked.
Attaches promise of light, healing, and answered prayer to such obedience.
Calls the people to honor the Sabbath and call it a delight.
scriptures: Isa 58:6
Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?
Isa 58:7

Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?

If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words:

Then shalt thou delight thyself in the LORD; and I will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth, and feed thee with the heritage of Jacob thy father: the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it.
corruption_summary: The chapter’s call to mercy is severed from its call to obedience and Sabbath, recruited for a social gospel without repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the unity of true religion: the same chapter that commands feeding the hungry and freeing the oppressed commands also honoring the Sabbath and turning from one’s own pleasure. Isaiah 58 will not be split into a gospel of social action without holiness, nor a gospel of private piety without mercy. The fast God chooses flows from a heart turned to Him and issues in both worship and works of love.

A common corruption mines the chapter for a social gospel that prizes justice-language while discarding repentance, Sabbath, and submission to God. But the works of mercy in Isaiah 58 are the fruit of a right relation to the LORD, not a substitute for it; they are joined inseparably to delighting in the holy day and honoring God above one’s own ways. The dictionary holds the whole chapter together: mercy without godliness is as empty as the fast God rejected, and godliness without mercy is the very hypocrisy He exposed.
roots_summary: The chapter contrasts the fast men choose with the fast God chooses, binding worship to mercy and Sabbath-keeping.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsōm — a fast, the affliction of the soul before God.
Hebrew ḥesed — covenant mercy, lovingkindness; the heart of the chosen fast.
Hebrew shabbāth — Sabbath, rest; called “a delight, the holy of the LORD.”
The “bands of wickedness” and “heavy burdens” picture oppression to be loosed.
The promised “high places of the earth” signify exaltation and blessing for the obedient.
usage: Isaiah 58 is preached on the nature of true fasting and sincere worship.
Its call to mercy is balanced by its call to Sabbath and obedience against a one-sided social gospel.
The chapter is cited to expose religious forms divorced from a changed heart.

etymology: The fifth chapter of Isaiah; containing the Song of the Vineyard and the six woes upon Judah.
biblical_def: Isaiah 5 contains the Song of the Vineyard and the six woes that follow it, a sustained indictment of Judah’s sin and a warning of judgment. The prophet sings of his Wellbeloved’s vineyard on a fruitful hill, which the owner fenced, cleared of stones, planted with the choicest vine, and furnished with a tower and a winepress, looking that it should bring forth grapes—but it brought forth wild grapes. The LORD then declares that He will take away its hedge and lay it waste, for “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant”; He looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry. There follow six woes against the sins of the nation: against those who join house to house and field to field in greed; against those who rise early to follow strong drink; against those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity and mock the LORD’s work; against those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light; against those wise in their own eyes; and against those who justify the wicked for reward. The chapter closes with the LORD whistling for a distant nation to come swiftly as the instrument of judgment. The dictionary receives Isaiah 5 as a solemn warning that privilege without fruit invites judgment, and that the perversion of moral categories—calling evil good and good evil—is among the surest marks of a people ripe for the LORD’s chastening.
webster_summary: Isaiah’s Song of the Vineyard and the six woes upon Judah; the LORD looked for fruit and found wild grapes, and warns of judgment on a people who call evil good and good evil.
webster_full: ISAIAH 5, the Song of the Vineyard and the six woes.
The LORD’s vineyard, the house of Israel, brought forth wild grapes instead of good.
He looked for judgment, but found oppression; for righteousness, but a cry.
Six woes against greed, drunkenness, defiance, moral inversion, pride, and bribery.
“Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil.”
scriptures: Isa 5:4
What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? wherefore, when I looked that it should bring forth grapes, brought it forth wild grapes?
Isa 5:7
For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.
Isa 5:20
Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
Isa 5:21
Woe unto them that are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight!
corruption_summary: The chapter’s woe against calling evil good and good evil is itself the diagnosis of an age that has inverted the moral order.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The chapter is itself the rebuke of the reigning corruption. Isaiah’s fifth woe—“Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness”—names precisely the inversion of moral categories that marks a culture in rebellion against God. To celebrate what Scripture condemns and to condemn what Scripture commends is not progress but the very sign of a people ripe for judgment.

The Song of the Vineyard adds a second warning against presuming on privilege. Judah had every advantage—the fence, the choicest vine, the tower, the winepress—yet brought forth wild grapes, and its privileges only deepened its guilt. The dictionary applies the lesson soberly: a church or nation richly favored with the means of grace, that yet brings forth oppression instead of righteousness, has more to fear, not less. The LORD looks for fruit, and where He finds none, He removes the hedge.
roots_summary: The chapter’s vineyard and woes set forth the LORD’s just judgment on a favored but fruitless people.
roots_lines: Hebrew kerem — vineyard; the figure for the house of Israel under the LORD’s care.
Hebrew be’ushim — wild or worthless grapes, the bitter fruit Judah yielded.
Hebrew hōy — woe; the lament that opens each of the six indictments.
The play on words: He looked for mishpāt (judgment) but found mispaḥ (oppression).
The vineyard image recurs in Christ’s parable of the wicked husbandmen.
usage: Isaiah 5’s woe against calling evil good is cited against modern moral inversion.
The Song of the Vineyard is preached on privilege, fruitlessness, and judgment.
The chapter is connected with Christ’s vineyard parables in the Gospels.
